author: Claude (EFL materials writer role)
basis: Draft 1 against the v2 quality gate.

slides.1: Our education system looks excellent on paper, but does it actually give every student the same chance? Today I want to test that question through the subject I know best: science.
slides.2: The fourth goal promises inclusive, lifelong learning. It should not matter what your family earns or where you live. Taiwan built a high-tech economy on that promise, yet we rarely ask whether our tools are ethical.
slides.3: Taiwan has invested in STEM for decades, and that money created our prosperity. Now the birth rate has fallen to a historic low. We should ask whether those resources reach the problems that matter most.
slides.4: Births have collapsed from 300,000 in 1990 to under 140,000 last year. Because of this, rural schools are shutting, and the students left behind must travel much further.
slides.5: In science lessons we spend our time memorizing answers for the exam, and creativity quietly disappears. Students who might have loved the subject drop it early. Will that habit help us solve something like climate change?
slides.6: City classrooms have modern laboratories, while remote schools share what little equipment they own. Official surveys put that resource gap at roughly 30%. Is our system built to close it, or to ignore it?
slides.7: Now for the achievements. Our 12 years of basic schooling cost families nothing, and 99% of children complete primary education. That puts us at the top of the OECD range, though access has never meant quality.
slides.8: Government subsidies now put 96% of disadvantaged five-year-olds into a preschool class. There they pick up the counting and the asking that science will later need. The gap starts to close before school has even begun.
slides.9: Our graduation rates beat the global average at every stage, and better teacher training has lifted what happens in the classroom. Yet high numbers can hide how far our regions differ.
slides.10: The response has started. Public money is now going into inquiry-based STEM courses, so a lesson means building something rather than reading about it. Children meet coding and AI ethics far earlier than we did.
slides.11: More than 80% of our schools now run digital lessons. Simulations let a class test an idea instead of standing in a lab, which links them to our semiconductor industry. But responsible use must be taught.
slides.12: Gifted students win internships with the big tech firms, where mentors give them projects that matter. The step from a lecture hall into a green-energy career is much shorter now.
slides.13: Science teaching feeds an export economy worth around 500 billion US dollars a year. The same skills also build the climate-ready infrastructure that a hotter, wetter island is going to need.
slides.14: Not everything here has improved. Women still take only 30% of engineering degrees, because the old idea that technology suits men has never quite died. Those old stereotypes cost us talent that we cannot spare.
slides.15: If we ignore these gaps, inequality will deepen and a whole generation of talent is wasted. As college students we should ask whether policy can keep pace with AI-driven work.
slides.16: Education decides how resilient a society can be. Without serious reform, though, Taiwan will slowly lose its edge in sustainable technology. Our science teaching has to keep up with the century that it serves.
slides.17: In summary, SDG 4 reveals both genuine progress and stubborn problems. STEM has become the engine of our development, and enrollment stays high. But we still have to make the system fair for every learner.
slides.18: Our test scores look impressive, yet they measure memory far better than imagination or fairness. Real reform means changing what we reward, not adding one more exam to the calendar.
slides.19: In future, inclusive STEM must reach the groups we usually overlook, and the curriculum needs a serious update. Every course should link what it teaches to real life outside the window.
slides.20: Here is the ask. Join the debate about school policy, volunteer where rural classrooms need help, or push your own department to change its curriculum. Taiwan can create an education system that leaves no one out.
